food.text: Dutch, English, and Danish whalers used the Arctic archipelago of Spitsbergen as a base in the 17th and 18th centuries, hunting bowhead whale there from 1611. The Dutch settlement of Smeerenburg, founded in 1619, became one of the first whaling stations, and by the early 1630s a few whalers had begun to overwinter there.

Starting in 1719 the Dutch began large-scale whaling in the Davis Strait, the waters between Greenland and Canada's Baffin Island. Britain's South Sea Company went on to finance 172 whaling voyages to Greenland from London's Howland Dock between 1725 and 1732.

Dutch Arctic whaling grew rapidly after Willem Barentsz's expedition discovered the archipelago of Spitsbergen, with the number of Dutch whaling ships more than doubling to 70 by 1654 and again to 148 by 1670. The booming whale trade helped make the Dutch Republic one of the richest nations of the 17th century, but the whales were ruthlessly exploited. By the mid-17th century the catches decreased as the favoured whales became rare.

Norse settlers in Greenland relied on livestock farming and hunting for their food, with farms spread far apart because of the large pasture areas the animals needed. Their settlements were dying out by the early 1500s, and when the German captain Gerd Mestemaker reached the west coast in 1541 he found no one still alive there.

The Dutch settlement of Smeerenburg on Spitsbergen, founded in 1619, was one of the first whaling bases built in the archipelago. The English, Danish, and French also built smaller bases. Because the area was lawless, English, Danish, Dutch, and French companies and authorities tried to use force to keep other countries' fleets out.

From 1733 the British government paid a bounty for whale oil brought back from Greenland's waters, encouraging the whaling fleet to expand further. Later cuts to the bounty and wars with America and France shrank London's Greenland whaling fleet to just 19 ships by 1796.

The Little Ice Age, which set in between 1400 and 1600, shortened the open-water season and reduced the number of whales in the High Arctic, limiting how much Thule hunters could hunt from boats. By the 16th century, hunting whales from umiak and kayak had ceased there entirely, pushing people to rely more on caribou, seal, and fish.

In 1604 an English ship landed at Bjørnøya, or Bear Island, south of Spitsbergen, and began hunting walrus there. By the late 17th century Russian hunters had also arrived in Svalbard, overwintering there to hunt land mammals such as polar bears and foxes.

Most crews on Dutch whaling ships bound for Greenland and Svalbard came from the Frisian Wadden Sea islands, especially Föhr, whose sailors were known as skilled mariners. At the height of Dutch whaling in 1762, 1,186 seamen from Föhr alone were serving aboard these vessels, and a quarter of all Dutch whaling ship captains came from the island.

By 1600, worsening cold brought on by the Little Ice Age had forced Thule communities to abandon the High Arctic entirely. Those living near open water were less affected by the falling temperatures, and this shift in circumstances contributed to the emergence of local groups such as the Copper Inuit and Netsilik.

art.text: The town of Sisimiut, on Greenland's west coast, still has the 1775 Bethel-kirken, also called Blå Kirke or the Blue Church. It is the oldest surviving church in Greenland.

In 1747 there were enough converts in Greenland to prompt construction of the Moravian Brethren Mission House. The mission was formally established as New Herrnhut. It became the nucleus of present-day Nuuk, as many Greenlanders from the southeastern coast moved to live at the mission station.

Among the 18th-century buildings still standing in Sisimiut is the 1725 Gammelhuset, meaning Old House. Like the Blue Church, it was moved from the former settlement site at Ukiivik (Holsteinsborg) together with the rest of the settlement.

A museum in Sisimiut holds an inventory from the Old Church, including the original altarpiece dated to approximately 1650. The museum's collection also includes tools and domestic items gathered between 1902 and 1922, and paintings from the 1790s.
Sisimiut's museum also displays paintings from the 1790s, alongside its collection of tools and domestic items gathered between 1902 and 1922 and its inventory from the Old Church.

The outdoor exhibition at Sisimiut's museum includes the remains of a kayak from the 18th century. The museum also holds the Poul Madsen collection, made up of handcraft, art, house items and ethnographic objects compiled over fifty years.

war.text: When Hans Egede founded the first Danish colonies in Greenland, Dutch whalers dominated the area around present-day Sisimiut. The Dutch were finally removed in a series of battles in 1738 and 1739.

In the early eighteenth century, Arctic indigenous societies began to buy guns from European traders. The guns increased hunting efficiency and led to a scarcity of resources in the region, a version of what Garrett Hardin called the tragedy of the commons.

Dutch whalers swiftly burnt down Hans Egede's Bergen Company whaling station on Nipisat Island. The island lies about 30 km north of present-day Sisimiut, and the Dutch held the upper hand in the area at the time.

The Dutch were only removed once Jacob Severin was granted a full monopoly on Greenlandic trade. He was also permitted to act as an agent of the Danish navy, and the battles of 1738 and 1739 followed.

literature.text: In classical and medieval literature, ultima Thule meant any distant place beyond the borders of the known world. By the Late Middle Ages and the early modern period, writers often identified the Greco-Roman Thule with the real Iceland or Greenland.

Two joiks, traditional Sámi songs, were recorded in Johannes Schefferus's Lapponia, published in 1673. They are among the earliest written documentation of Sámi oral poetry. More systematic collection of this poetry only took place in the 19th century.

A marriage certificate written at Garðar in Greenland in 1409 survives only in an Icelandic transcription made in 1625. Bishop Oddur Einarsson attested the copy, and it is considered reliable. It is one of the few non-runic texts that may preserve traits of Greenlandic Norse.

The English poet Ambrose Philips began a poem about the Fable of Thule but never completed it. He published the unfinished work in 1748, at a time when Thule was often identified with Iceland or Greenland.

The 1409 Garðar document was issued by two Greenland-based priests. It attested the banns for two Icelanders who had been blown off course to Greenland, Þorsteinn Ólafsson and Sigríður Björnsdóttir. The 1625 copy is how their story survives.

In 1721 the Lutheran missionary Hans Egede wrote of a blonde, "quite handsome and white" indigenous tribe he had discovered in Greenland. Adolphus Greely later published this eyewitness account among sightings of fair-haired Arctic natives gathered from earlier written literature.

The municipal archives of Hamburg hold a contemporary report about a voyage by a Hanseatic ship to Greenland. Its captain, Gerd Mestemaker, reached the west coast in 1541 but "couldn't get to anyone alive" there. Such written reports fed Europe's long uncertainty about the fate of the Norse settlers.

The language of the 1409 Greenland document is clearly not Icelandic. It uses the form þil instead of the older til, showing that initial 'þ' and 't' had merged. This matches the runic evidence for Greenlandic Norse and suggests writers who were Norwegian-educated but influenced by Greenlandic.

Adolphus Greely traced the first written sighting of light-haired Arctic natives to 1656. A Dutch trading vessel sailed west from Greenland across the Davis Strait toward Baffin Island. Its captain, Nicholas Tunes, claimed to have seen two distinct races, the brownish-skinned Inuit and a tall, fair-skinned people.

science.text: In 1500 King Manuel I of Portugal sent Gaspar Corte-Real to Greenland to look for a Northwest Passage to Asia. The cartographic information he supplied was built into a world map that Alberto Cantino presented to Ercole I d'Este in 1502. The Cantino planisphere, made in Lisbon, accurately depicts Greenland's southern coastline.

Early cartographers had little information and were unsure how to draw the region around the North Pole. Johannes Ruysch's map of 1507 and Gerardus Mercator's map of 1595 included land there, while Martin Waldseemüller's 1507 world map showed the whole region as water.

The English explorer John Davis charted Greenland's western coast as far north as Disko Bay during his 1585 and 1586 expeditions. English and Dutch whalers were so influential that, for a time, the island's western shore itself became known as 'Davis Strait'.

Few expeditions of the era went much beyond the Arctic Circle, and those that did added only small islands, such as Spitzbergen in 1596. From the late 16th century, expeditions to the Arctic Ocean became more common, often seeking trade routes from Europe to the Pacific Ocean. Geographical knowledge of the region gradually improved.

King Christian IV sent three expeditions to Greenland from 1605 to 1607, with James Hall as pilot on all of them. They were mostly unsuccessful because the leaders lacked Arctic ice experience. They were also told to search the east coast north of Cape Farewell, which is almost inaccessible because of southward-drifting ice.
Carl Linnaeus formally described the Arctic fox in the 10th edition of Systema Naturae in 1758, naming it Canis lagopus. The type specimen was recovered from Lapland, Sweden.

South-drifting icebergs during the Little Ice Age long made Greenland's eastern coast unreachable. This led to general confusion between Baffin Island, Greenland and Spitsbergen. The Frobisher 'Strait' was not confirmed to be a bay until 1861.

Martin Frobisher "rediscovered" Greenland in 1578. This prompted King Frederick II of Denmark to outfit an expedition of his own the next year under the Englishman James Alday. It proved a costly failure.

In the early eighteenth century, Arctic indigenous societies began buying guns from European traders. The guns increased hunting efficiency but led to a scarcity of resources, a version of what the human ecologist Garrett Hardin called 'the tragedy of the commons'.
Linnaeus's species name for the Arctic fox, lagopus, comes from the Ancient Greek words for 'hare' and 'foot'. It refers to the hair on the fox's feet, which resembles that of cold-climate hares.

politics.text: Denmark–Norway apparently believed the medieval Norse settlements in Greenland still survived. It kept claiming sovereignty over the island even though there had been no contact with the Norse for a very long time.

In 1775, when the United States was still a colony of the United Kingdom, Denmark–Norway declared Greenland a colony. This followed the 18th-century arrival of missionaries and traders from Denmark–Norway, who began recolonizing southern Greenland.

politics.text: Between 1605 and 1607, King Christian IV of Denmark and Norway sent three expeditions to Greenland and Arctic waterways. Their goals were to locate the lost eastern Norse settlement and to assert Danish-Norwegian sovereignty over Greenland. The expeditions were mostly unsuccessful.

In 1721, aspiring to become a colonial power, Denmark-Norway sent a missionary expedition to Greenland. This came after centuries in which the crown had apparently believed the old Norse settlements had survived, and it kept claiming sovereignty over the island.

In 1500, King Manuel I of Portugal sent Gaspar Corte-Real to Greenland to look for a Northwest Passage to Asia. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas, that region was considered part of Portugal's sphere of influence. Corte-Real returned in 1501 with his brother Miguel.

Denmark–Norway asserted Norway's territorial claims to Greenland after the Danish and Norwegian realms united in 1537. When the two separated in 1814, Greenland was kept by Denmark under the Treaty of Kiel.

politics.text: Denmark-Norway apparently believed the Norse settlements had survived and kept claiming sovereignty over Greenland despite a lack of contact. In 1721 it sent a missionary expedition to reinstate Christianity among the Norse descendants. No Norse were found, so the missionaries baptized the Inuit instead.
Most of the old Norse records concerning Greenland were removed from Trondheim to Copenhagen in 1664. They were subsequently lost, probably in the Copenhagen Fire of 1728.

philosophy.text: The arrival of Christian missionaries in the 18th century led to the suppression of Greenlandic drum dances, which were deemed pagan. They were replaced by polyphonic choral singing, influenced by German hymns from the Herrnhuter Brüdergemeinde.

In Europe, narwhal tusks were highly sought after for centuries, because of a medieval belief that they were the horns of the legendary unicorn. Considered to have magical properties, they were used to counter poisoning and all sorts of diseases, such as measles and rubella. The rise of modern science towards the end of the 17th century led to a decreased belief in magic and alchemy.

Nuuk was founded in 1728 by the Danish-Norwegian missionary Hans Egede, who moved there from the earlier Hope Colony, where he had arrived in 1721. The new colony was built at the Inuit settlement of Nûk and named Godthaab, meaning 'good hope'. The governor Claus Paarss was part of the relocation, and his colonists were mutinous soldiers, convicts and prostitutes. Within the first year most of them died of scurvy and other ailments.

Traditional Inuit theology holds that humans have two souls, one of which can journey out of the body. Ritual specialists called angakut mediated between humanity and the spirits. They performed rituals for healing, to recover lost objects, or to assist the hunt.

In 1721, Denmark–Norway sent a missionary expedition to Greenland to reinstate Christianity among the descendants of the Norse settlers. No Norse were found, so the missionaries baptized the Inuit inhabitants instead.

A smallpox epidemic in 1733 and 1734 killed most of the native population as well as Hans Egede's wife. This came after the colony's first year, when most of Claus Paarss's colonists, mutinous soldiers, convicts and prostitutes, had already died of scurvy and other ailments. Egede returned to Denmark in 1736 after 15 years in Greenland, leaving his son Poul to continue his missionary work.

In 1733, Moravian missionaries received permission to begin a mission in Greenland. By 1747 there were enough converts to justify building the Moravian Brethren Mission House and formally founding the mission as New Herrnhut. Many Greenlanders from the southeastern coast moved to live at the mission station.

Ethnographic accounts from the Inughuit of northern Greenland and the Labrador Inuit describe a recurring belief that ghosts and spirits may visit a person through their dreams. Dreams were generally deemed religiously significant and sometimes prophetic.

From the Moravian base at New Herrnhut, further missions were founded at Lichtenfels in 1748 and Lichtenau in 1774. The Moravian network grew in the decades after the first converts gathered at the mission station.

Only angakut of considerable ability were thought able to travel to other realms in spirit form. Audiences might sing to encourage them on their way. West Greenlandic legends told how these soul-travellers were repeatedly almost captured by the dangerous spirit Amarsiniook.

culture.text: The Inuit lived in a land where agriculture was never possible, so hunting became the core of their culture. They used harpoons and bows and arrows to take down animals of all sizes, and made fur clothing to survive the extreme climate.

The Little Ice Age, from 1550 to 1880, brought temperatures well below today's. Entire regions of the high Arctic were depopulated, partly by mass migrations and partly by the starvation of whole communities. The traditional way of life survived mainly in the more hospitable southern Baffin Island, Labrador and southern Greenland.

Inuit were first exposed to Christian Europeans in the 16th century. Missionaries worked among them over the following centuries. Their efforts led to a substantial decline in the angakut and various other Inuit traditions.

Greenlandic culture blends traditional Inuit and Scandinavian culture. The Kalaallit are known for figures called tupilak, meaning 'spirit object'. Sperm whale ivory remains a valued medium for carving.

The Little Ice Age shortened the season for open-water whale hunting. By the 16th century, umiak and kayak whale hunting had ceased in the High Arctic. By 1600 the people had abandoned the High Arctic, and local groups such as the Copper Inuit, Netsilik and Inglulingmuit emerged.
